new_entities.name: Pre-exercise caffeine intake
new_entities.description: Caffeine consumed before exercise in ergogenic doses.

new_entities.name: Endurance performance in trained athletes
aliases: cycling or running performance in trained athletes
new_entities.description: Performance in endurance exercise tasks among trained runners, cyclists, or other endurance-trained athletes.

edges.effect_quant: In trained runners, caffeine increases time to exhaustion with a pooled Hedges g of 0.344 (95% CI 0.122 to 0.566), and in trained cyclists moderate doses around 4 to 6 mg/kg improve time-trial performance by an SMD of -0.55 (95% CI -0.84 to -0.26).
edges.population: trained cyclists, trained runners, and endurance-trained adults
edges.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, lowering perceived effort and helping trained athletes sustain a harder pace for longer. In endurance settings that often shows up as slightly longer time to exhaustion or slightly faster completion times rather than a dramatic physiological transformation.
edges.summary: This is a fairly dependable ergogenic edge in trained endurance athletes. The clearest pooled evidence shows small but repeatable improvements in trained runners and cyclists, and direct cyclist trials suggest that the benefit persists even in people who already have a strong endurance base.
edges.caveats: The effect is modest and depends on dose, event type, heat stress, and habitual caffeine exposure. Not every trained athlete improves, and the benefit is easier to see in time-trial or time-to-exhaustion outcomes than in every endurance task.

evidence.notes: Effects of Caffeine Intake on Endurance Running Performance and Time to Exhaustion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: caffeine versus placebo for time to exhaustion in trained runners
